content: 1. The term low-calorie beverages in this study was determined to primarily, if not entirely, consist of beverages sweetened with non-sugar sweeteners (NSS). 2. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) conducted by Engel et al. in 2018 examined the effects of consuming high milk and sugar-sweetened beverages versus non-caloric soft drinks on insulin sensitivity over six months in overweight and obese adults. The study was published in the European Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 3. The WHO guideline annex references a study by Viveros-Watty et al. (2021) that investigated the effects of reducing artificially sweetened beverage consumption on cardiometabolic risk factors in overweight individuals. This was a randomized controlled trial published in Endocrinology, Diabetes & Nutrition. 4. Maersk et al. (2012) conducted a six-month randomized intervention study that demonstrated sucrose-sweetened beverages increased fat storage in the liver, muscle, and visceral fat depots. This study was published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition. 5. Davis et al. (2018) found that the consumption of artificially sweetened beverages was associated with increased adiposity and higher HbA1c levels in Hispanic youth. This study was published in Clinical Obesity. 6. Cocco et al. (2019) conducted a double-blind RCT to evaluate the effects of daily snacks containing maltitol or stevia rebaudiana as sweeteners on dental caries risk in high-caries-risk schoolchildren. The study was published in Oral Health & Preventive Dentistry. 7. Vandana et al. (2017) assessed the effectiveness of stevia as a mouth rinse among 12–15-year-old schoolchildren in Andhra Pradesh, India, through a randomized controlled trial. The findings were published in the Journal of the Indian Society of Periodontology. 8. Marshall et al. (2003) explored the relationship between dental caries and beverage consumption in young children. This study was published in Pediatrics. 9. Taljaard et al. (2013) investigated the effects of a multi-micronutrient-fortified beverage, with and without sugar, on growth and cognition in South African schoolchildren. This randomized, double-blind, controlled intervention was published in the British Journal of Nutrition. 10. Striegel-Moore et al. (2006) examined the correlates of beverage intake in adolescent girls as part of the National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute Growth and Health Study. The findings were published in the Journal of Pediatrics. 11. Cohen et al. (2018) studied the associations between prenatal and child sugar intake and child cognition. This research was published in the American Journal of Preventive Medicine. 12. Günther et al. (2019) conducted a secondary analysis of the cluster-randomized GeliS trial to investigate associations between prenatal diet and neonatal outcomes. The study was published in Nutrients. 13. Salavati et al. (2020) analyzed data from a population-based birth cohort to explore the relationship between maternal preconception food group intake and offspring birth weight. This study was published in Nutrients. 14. Munda et al. (2019) examined the association between pre-pregnancy body weight and dietary patterns with the likelihood of large-for-gestational-age infants in gestational diabetes. The findings were published in Diabetology & Metabolic Syndrome. 15. Azad et al. (2016) investigated the association between artificially sweetened beverage consumption during pregnancy and infant body mass index. This study was published in JAMA Pediatrics. 16. Gillman et al. (2017) explored the relationship between beverage intake during pregnancy and childhood adiposity. The findings were published in Pediatrics. 17. Zhu et al. (2017) conducted a prospective cohort study to assess maternal consumption of artificially sweetened beverages during pregnancy and offspring growth through seven years of age. This study was published in the International Journal of Epidemiology. 18. The WHO guideline annex highlights that the use of NSS was compared to lower or no NSS intake, as well as the replacement of sugars with NSS. The main outcomes assessed included body weight, energy and sugar intake, and non-communicable diseases (NCDs). 19. Overweight and obesity are significant global health concerns, with 9 billion adults aged 18 years and older being overweight, of which more than 600 million are obese. In 2020, over 38 million children under five years of age were overweight, marking an increase of approximately 6 million over the past 20 years. 20. High body mass index (BMI) was responsible for an estimated 4 million deaths in 2017, with increases in BMI within the overweight and obesity range leading to a greater risk of mortality. Overweight and obesity are also risk factors for numerous NCDs, including cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), type 2 diabetes, and certain cancers. 21. The NUGAG Subgroup on Diet and Health concluded that short-term weight loss observed in RCTs of varied design does not constitute a health benefit. Evidence for reduced energy and sugar intake, which also came from short-term trials, was not considered a desirable effect unless it contributed to weight loss or healthy weight maintenance. 22. The subgroup determined that the effects of NSS on body weight are uncertain. Observed effects were small (body weight, BMI) to moderate (energy intake, sugar intake). However, the heterogeneity of RCT designs and the relatively short trial durations limit the reliability of these findings. 23. For children, the subgroup also concluded that the effects of NSS on body weight are uncertain. Two RCTs reported desirable effects on dental caries, but the size of these effects was unclear. 24. For pregnant women, no specific desirable effects of NSS use were identified. 25. Undesirable effects of NSS use in adults were primarily observed in prospective cohort studies. These effects varied from small to moderate and included an increased total cholesterol-to-HDL cholesterol ratio and a moderate increased risk of bladder cancer. 26. The overall certainty of evidence for NSS effects in adults, children, and pregnant women was rated as low. For adults, the certainty was low for outcomes such as body weight, BMI, energy intake, sugar intake, and type 2 diabetes. For children, the certainty was moderate for body weight and BMI z-scores but low for dental caries. 27. The subgroup concluded that the potential long-term undesirable effects of NSS use outweigh any short-term benefits, such as small reductions in body weight and BMI observed in RCTs. 28. Limited evidence suggests that NSS use may have beneficial effects on dental caries in children, but these effects are primarily due to the displacement of free sugars rather than any inherent properties of NSS. 29. The subgroup emphasized that reductions in free sugar intake can be achieved without the use of NSS, thereby avoiding potential long-term adverse effects associated with NSS use. 30. The evidence from prospective studies of pregnant women suggests that potential adverse effects of NSS use may occur over the relatively short period of gestation. 31. The subgroup concluded that the balance of effects likely favors not using NSS, as the potential undesirable effects outweigh the limited short-term benefits.
